events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1956, the last British troops departed from Egypt, marking the end of British military presence in the country following the Suez Crisis. This event was a significant milestone in Egypt's journey towards full sovereignty.
events.name: Last British troops leave Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1956, playwright Arthur Miller appeared before the House Un-American Activities Committee in Washington, D.C., where he faced questioning about his political beliefs and associations. This event highlighted the tensions between art and politics during the Red Scare.
events.name: Arthur Miller appears before the House Un-American Activities Committee

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1956, Gamal Abdel Nasser was officially declared the second president of Egypt, a position he would hold until his death in 1970. Nasser's presidency was marked by significant social and economic reforms, as well as a strong stance against colonialism.
events.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser becomes president of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1956, labor riots erupted in Poznań, Poland, resulting in a violent crackdown by Soviet troops, who fired on protesters demanding better working conditions and political reforms. The protests and subsequent repression highlighted the growing discontent in Eastern Europe during the Cold War.
events.name: Poznań 1956 protests

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1956, iconic actress Marilyn Monroe married renowned playwright Arthur Miller in a private ceremony in White Plains, New York. Their union was highly publicized and symbolized a significant cultural moment in American history, reflecting the intersection of Hollywood glamour and literary prestige.

locations.name: White Plains, New York, United States

events.name: Marilyn Monroe marries Arthur Miller

Their union was highly publicized and symbolized a significant cultural moment in American history, reflecting the intersection of Hollywood glamour and literary prestige.

locations.name: White Plains, New York, United States

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1956, a tragic mid-air collision occurred over the Grand Canyon involving a TWA Lockheed Constellation and a United Airlines Douglas DC-7, resulting in the deaths of all 128 passengers and crew aboard both aircraft. This disaster prompted significant reforms in aviation safety regulations and air traffic control in the United States.

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1956, a laboratory experiment involving scrap thorium at Sylvania Electric Products in Bayside, New York, resulted in a significant explosion. This incident raised concerns about safety protocols in laboratories handling radioactive materials.
events.name: Thorium explosion at Sylvania Electric Products

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1956, an American Lockheed U-2 reconnaissance aircraft made its inaugural flight over the Soviet Union. This event marked a significant advancement in aerial surveillance technology during the Cold War, enhancing intelligence-gathering capabilities.
events.name: First flight of Lockheed U-2 over Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1956, an Austrian expedition achieved the first ascent of Gasherbrum II, one of the highest peaks in the Karakoram range, located on the border between Pakistan and China. This accomplishment contributed to the history of mountaineering and exploration in the region.

events.name: First ascent of Gasherbrum II

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1956, a powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck the Cyclades island group in the Aegean Sea, causing widespread destruction and resulting in 53 fatalities. The earthquake's intensity and subsequent tsunami highlighted the geological volatility of the region.
events.name: Amorgos earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1956, the British House of Lords voted against the abolition of the death penalty, reflecting the ongoing debate over capital punishment in the United Kingdom. This decision underscored the complexities of legal and moral considerations surrounding the issue.
events.name: British House of Lords defeats death penalty abolition

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1956, a pivotal conference on artificial intelligence was held at Dartmouth College, organized by prominent figures including John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky. This meeting laid the groundwork for the field of AI, fostering collaboration and innovation among leading researchers.

locations.name: Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, United States

events.name: Dartmouth Conference on Artificial Intelligence

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1956, the Italian ocean liner SS Andrea Doria sank after colliding with the Swedish ship SS Stockholm in heavy fog off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, resulting in the deaths of 51 people. This maritime disaster became a significant event in maritime history, prompting changes in safety regulations.
events.name: Sinking of SS Andrea Doria

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1956, Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser announced the nationalization of the Suez Canal, a move that sparked international condemnation and led to the Suez Crisis. This pivotal event marked a significant moment in post-colonial history and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
events.name: Nasser nationalizes the Suez Canal

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1956, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed a joint resolution of Congress officially adopting 'In God We Trust' as the national motto of the United States. This decision reflected the growing influence of religion in American public life during the Cold War era.

image.caption: Enlargement of a $20 bill displaying the motto “In God We Trust.”
image.credit: The original uploader was Themanwithoutapast at English Wikipedia . — Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by PhiLiP using CommonsHelper .
image.date_qualification: A depiction of the motto on U.S. currency, not the 1956 congressional authorization event. The image date is the original upload date, not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Congress authorizes 'In God We Trust' as national motto

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1956, cricketer Jim Laker achieved an extraordinary feat by taking 19 wickets in a first-class match at Old Trafford during the fourth Test between England and Australia. This remarkable performance set a new record in cricket history, surpassing the previous best of 17 wickets.
events.name: Jim Laker sets record in cricket

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1956, cricketer Jim Laker achieved an extraordinary feat by taking 19 wickets in a first-class match at Old Trafford during the fourth Test between England and Australia. This remarkable performance set a new record in cricket history, surpassing the previous best of 17 wickets.
events.name: Jim Laker sets record in cricket (duplicate)

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1956, a catastrophic explosion occurred in Cali, Colombia, when seven ammunition trucks loaded with dynamite detonated, resulting in an estimated death toll ranging from 1,300 to 10,000 people. This disaster highlighted the dangers of inadequate safety measures in urban areas.
events.name: Explosion of ammunition trucks in Cali

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1956, a devastating fire broke out at the Bois du Cazier coal mine in Marcinelle, Belgium, claiming the lives of 262 miners, predominantly Italian nationals. This tragedy underscored the perilous working conditions in the mining industry during that era.
events.name: Bois du Cazier coal mine fire

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1956, the influential art exhibition 'This Is Tomorrow' opened at the Whitechapel Art Gallery in London. This exhibition showcased innovative works by contemporary artists and played a pivotal role in the development of the British pop art movement.
events.name: This Is Tomorrow art exhibition opens

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1956, approximately 5,000 members of the Romanian Greek-Catholic Church gathered outside the Piarists' Church in Cluj-Napoca to hold a mass, demonstrating their resilience against government repression. This event highlighted the ongoing struggle for religious freedom in Romania.
events.name: Mass by Romanian Greek-Catholic Church

events.enhanced_description: On August 17, 1956, West Germany enacted a ban on the Communist Party of Germany, reflecting the heightened tensions of the Cold War and the government's efforts to suppress communist influence within the country. This decision was part of a broader strategy to maintain political stability.
events.name: West Germany bans Communist Party

events.enhanced_description: The Ein Ofarim killings on September 12, 1956, involved an attack on Israeli Druze civilians by Palestinian fedayeen. This event was part of the ongoing violence and conflict in the region during the mid-20th century.
events.name: Ein Ofarim killings

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1956, an IBM team led by Reynold B. Johnson invented the hard disk drive, revolutionizing data storage technology. This innovation paved the way for the development of modern computing and data management systems.
events.name: Invention of the hard disk drive

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1956, television broadcasting officially began in Australia, marking a significant milestone in the country's media landscape. The introduction of television transformed entertainment and information dissemination across the nation.
events.name: Television broadcasting in Australia commences

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1956, Nicaraguan dictator Anastasio Somoza García was assassinated, an event that marked a turning point in Nicaraguan politics. His death led to a power struggle and eventually contributed to the rise of the Sandinista movement.
events.name: Assassination of Anastasio Somoza García

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1956, the submarine transatlantic telephone cable was opened, significantly enhancing global communication capabilities. This technological advancement allowed for more efficient and reliable telephone connections between North America and Europe.
events.name: Opening of the submarine transatlantic telephone cable

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1956, the Bell X-2 became the first crewed aircraft to reach Mach 3, demonstrating the potential for high-speed flight. This achievement contributed to advancements in aerospace technology and research.
events.name: Bell X-2 reaches Mach 3

events.enhanced_description: The Polish October of 1956 marked a period of political liberalization and destalinization in Poland, leading to the rise of Władysław Gomułka as the leader who promised reforms. This movement was part of a broader wave of de-Stalinization across Eastern Europe, reflecting the desire for greater autonomy from Soviet control.
events.name: Polish October

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1956, a group of Palestinian Arab fedayeen ambushed Israeli civilians traveling on Highway 25 in the Negev Desert, resulting in casualties and escalating tensions in the region. This incident was part of the broader context of conflict surrounding the Suez Crisis and the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian tensions.
events.name: Negev desert road ambush

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1956, Cecil B. DeMille's epic film 'The Ten Commandments' premiered in the United States, featuring Charlton Heston as Moses. The film became one of the highest-grossing films of all time, celebrated for its grand scale and production.
events.name: Release of The Ten Commandments film

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1956, Don Larsen of the New York Yankees pitched the only perfect game in World Series history during Game 5 against the Brooklyn Dodgers. This remarkable feat solidified his place in baseball history and earned him the series MVP.
events.name: Don Larsen's perfect game in World Series

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1956, Finland officially joined UNESCO, committing to international cooperation in education, science, and culture. This membership marked Finland's dedication to promoting global cultural and educational initiatives.
events.name: Finland joins UNESCO

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1956, B. R. Ambedkar, a prominent Dalit leader, converted to Buddhism in Nagpur, India, along with 385,000 followers. This mass conversion was a significant event in the Dalit Buddhist movement, symbolizing a quest for social equality.
events.name: B. R. Ambedkar converts to Buddhism

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1956, the British Royal Air Force retired its last Avro Lancaster bomber, marking the end of an era for one of World War II's most iconic aircraft. The Lancaster played a crucial role in various operations during the war.
events.name: Retirement of the last Avro Lancaster bomber

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1956, Calder Hall in Sellafield, Cumbria, became the world's first industrial-scale commercial nuclear power plant. This landmark development marked a significant step in the use of nuclear energy for electricity generation.
events.name: Opening of Calder Hall nuclear power plant

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1956, the Soviet–Japanese Joint Declaration was signed in Moscow, officially ending the legal state of war between the Soviet Union and Japan. This agreement paved the way for the restoration of diplomatic relations between the two nations.
events.name: Soviet–Japanese Joint Declaration of 1956

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1956, the Hungarian Revolution broke out in Budapest as a student demonstration against the pro-Soviet government. This uprising aimed to establish a more democratic government and sought to withdraw Hungary from the Warsaw Pact.
events.name: Hungarian Revolution of 1956

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1956, the Protocol of Sèvres was signed, a secret agreement between Israel, France, and the United Kingdom. This pact facilitated Israel's invasion of the Sinai Peninsula, leading to the Suez Crisis.
events.name: Protocol of Sèvres signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1956, Soviet Red Army troops invaded Hungary in response to the ongoing revolution. This military intervention aimed to suppress the uprising and reassert Soviet control over the country.
events.name: Soviet invasion of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1956, during the Suez Crisis, Israel launched an invasion of the Sinai Peninsula, pushing Egyptian forces back toward the Suez Canal. This military action was part of a coordinated effort with France and the UK to regain control over the canal.

image.caption: A Royal Navy Hawker Sea Hawk FGA.6 of 899 Naval Air Squadron, armed with rockets, aboard HMS Eagle.
image.credit: Royal Navy official photographer — This photograph A 33616 comes from the collections of the Imperial War Museums .
image.date_qualification: November 1956; the saved image date is month-only and does not establish the date of the specific strike.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Suez Crisis: Israel invades the Sinai Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1956, the United Kingdom and France began bombing Egypt in an attempt to force the reopening of the Suez Canal during the Suez Crisis. This military intervention escalated tensions in the region and drew international condemnation.
events.name: Suez Crisis: UK and France bomb Egypt

events.enhanced_description: The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 was a landmark legislation that reorganized the boundaries and names of Indian states based on linguistic and cultural lines. This act led to the formation of three new states: Kerala, Karnataka, and Andhra Pradesh.

image.caption: Map showing South Indian state boundaries before the States Reorganisation Act.
